Prefill-decode disaggregation splits the two computationally distinct phases of LLM inference onto separate worker pools — prefill workers handle the prompt's quadratic attention computation, decode workers handle the sequential, memory-bandwidth-bound token generation — and the central question is: how does KV cache reuse (prefix caching) interact with this split when requests arrive with heterogeneous cache hit rates and asymmetric priority tiers? The naive assumption is that a high cache-hit request is "cheaper" and should move through the system faster, but in a disaggregated setting the KV cache lives on the prefill worker and must be either transferred to the decode worker or the decode worker must be colocated with the cache — neither is free. The expert's first worry is KV transfer bandwidth becoming the hidden bottleneck: a high-priority, low-cache-hit request can saturate the interconnect between prefill and decode pools, stalling high-hit requests that nominally needed almost no compute but still require their cached KV tensors to be present on the decode side. The second, subtler worry is priority inversion under asymmetric batching pressure: decode workers accumulate a backlog of low-priority, long-running sequences that hold memory, and when a high-priority prefill completes and pushes its KV transfer, there may be no decode slot available — the scheduling policies governing prefill admission, KV eviction, and decode slot reservation are typically designed independently and fail to compose correctly at the boundary. The beginner sees two clean pools and expects isolation; the expert sees a coupled system where cache residency decisions, transfer scheduling, and batch slot management must be co-designed or you get pathological latency spikes precisely on the requests you most wanted to protect.

When prefill completes but no decode slot is free, the KV cache has four concrete landing zones. Stay on the prefill worker's GPU HBM: simplest, zero transfer cost, but the prefill worker's memory is now pinched — Splitwise (Patel et al., 2023) explicitly identifies this as a capacity hazard where prefill workers become decode-memory sinks, degrading their own batching efficiency and creating head-of-line blocking for subsequent prefills. Transfer speculatively to a decode worker's HBM anyway and queue there: this wins if a slot opens quickly, but if the decode worker is under sustained pressure the KV tensors sit in HBM consuming ~2MB per token per layer (at fp16, 40-layer model) while the decode worker's batch is already memory-capacity-bound — you've paid the transfer cost and gained nothing. Spill to CPU DRAM on either worker: DistServe and Mooncake both explore this; PCIe bandwidth (~64 GB/s bidirectional on NVLink-adjacent configs, far less on standard x16 PCIe) means a 32k-token KV cache can take tens of milliseconds to reload, which violates tight TTFT+TPOT SLO contracts for the very high-priority requests you're trying to protect. Evict and recompute on admission: cleanest memory accounting, but recomputation cost scales quadratically with prompt length — a 16k-token prompt at 40 layers recomputes in hundreds of milliseconds, catastrophic for a tier-1 request. The failure mode that cuts across all options is the absence of a global arbiter: prefill workers make local eviction decisions without knowing decode slot availability timelines, so every option degrades gracefully in isolation but catastrophically under coordinated load.

The strongest practical estimator is a per-sequence remaining-length posterior updated online via a learned output-length predictor, as explored in Zheng et al.'s Orca successor work and concretely implemented in vLLM's recent preemption scheduling experiments — the key insight is that output length distributions are heavy-tailed and strongly conditioned on request type (chat completions cluster near 200-400 tokens; code completions spike multimodally), so a mixture-of-distributions model trained on request metadata (system prompt fingerprint, prompt length, user tier) substantially outperforms a flat exponential decay assumption. The failure mode of using a mean estimator is precisely the heavy tail: the mean release time for a decode slot occupied by a long-context summarization request can be 3-5× the median, so the arbiter systematically underestimates slot occupancy for exactly the requests that hold slots longest, causing it to over-commit KV transfer slots and generate transfer collisions at the decode worker. A quantile estimator targeting P75 or P80 of remaining decode time is a better arbiter primitive — it biases toward conservative slot forecasts, reducing collisions at the cost of slight under-utilization, and this conservatism interacts cleanly with priority tiers because high-priority requests can be granted transfers on optimistic (P50) forecasts while low-priority requests use pessimistic (P90) forecasts, creating an implicit priority-weighted admission window. The dangerous interaction is priority tier collapse under misprediction: if a high-priority request is admitted on a P50 forecast that proves wrong, its KV tensors arrive to a full decode worker and must be held somewhere, consuming exactly the buffer capacity that low-priority requests were already filling — the optimistic estimator for high-priority requests can paradoxically worsen their realized latency relative to a flat conservative policy. Google's PaLM serving infrastructure (as described in the 2023 MLSys efficiency talks) addresses this by coupling the output-length predictor to an admission controller that reserves a decode slot before prefill even begins, making the forecast's consequence deterministic rather than probabilistic — but this requires knowing the assigned decode worker at prefill admission time, which re-couples the two pools and partially undermines the disaggregation benefit.

The immediate recovery options when a reserved decode worker fails mid-prefill are: re-reserve on a surviving worker and transfer partial KV cache, checkpoint the prefill state and restart on a new worker pair, or abort and requeue the request — and the correct choice depends on how far prefill has progressed, because partial KV tensors for a 50%-complete prefill represent real compute already spent, making abort-and-requeue increasingly expensive as prompt length grows. The naive re-reservation protocol exposes the first deep coupling: to transfer partial KV tensors to a new decode worker, the prefill worker must know which layers have been computed, the new decode worker must have contiguous HBM available matching the partial tensor size, and the arbiter must atomically update its slot map — three-way coordination that must complete before the prefill worker's next forward pass, imposing a synchronization barrier that local-decision systems never faced. What this reveals is that KV cache identity is coupled to worker identity in a way that pure disaggregation rhetoric obscures: in systems like Mooncake that use a distributed KV cache store (essentially a disaggregated memory tier separate from both prefill and decode workers), partial-prefill recovery becomes a metadata update rather than a tensor migration, but you've now introduced a third failure domain — the KV store itself — whose availability becomes a prerequisite for both pools. The recovery protocol also surfaces priority inversion at the reservation layer: when a new decode slot is grabbed for the recovering high-priority request, it must either preempt an existing low-priority decode sequence (requiring KV eviction or CPU spill of that sequence's state) or wait for natural slot release, and most systems have no preemption path at the decode slot level because it was never needed in coupled architectures. Splitwise's evaluation showed that worker failure rates of even 0.1% at their operating scale generated enough mid-prefill orphans to require explicit protocol design — they concluded that the "clean separation" of prefill and decode pools is an architectural fiction maintained only when both pools are fully healthy, and the recovery protocol is where the true coupling re-emerges. The fundamental revelation is that prefill and decode pools share logical state (the KV cache) even when physically separated, and any failure that disrupts the handoff protocol forces the system to choose between re-coupling the pools operationally or accepting the compute waste of recomputation — disaggregation buys efficiency in the common case but exports coupling cost into the failure handling path.

Standard LRU fails here for a structural reason: LRU treats recency of last access as a proxy for future access probability, but prefill and decode access patterns have opposite temporal signatures — a prefill access is a one-shot write followed by a single read (when the decode worker fetches it), while a decode access is a repeated incremental append across potentially thousands of steps, meaning LRU will evict "cold" prefill-written entries that are actually about to be read imminently while retaining "warm" decode-appended entries whose sequence is nearly complete and will never be reused. The correct policy needs to be access-pattern-aware with a phase classifier: entries written by prefill workers should be tagged with an expected fetch deadline (derived from the arbiter's slot reservation schedule), and the eviction priority should be based on time-to-fetch rather than time-since-last-access — an entry written 500ms ago with a fetch deadline 10ms away is maximally valuable and should be the last evicted, not the first. Priority tiers add a second dimension: eviction should be priority-weighted such that a tier-1 request's KV tensors carry an eviction cost multiplier, analogous to weighted caching as formalized in the file caching literature (Young 1994; more recently in ML contexts by Cao et al.'s GLCache work), so the optimizer trades off evicting many low-priority tensors before touching a single high-priority one. The asymmetric size structure also matters: a full prefill KV cache for a 32k-token prompt at fp16 across 40 layers is roughly 160GB (2 bytes × 2 × 40 layers × 32768 tokens × 4096 dim / tensor-parallel factor), dwarfing the incremental decode appends per step (~4KB per token), so a size-aware eviction term is necessary to prevent large prefill tensors from dominating eviction decisions purely due to their byte footprint. Mooncake's OPEX paper proposes deadline-aware priority eviction (DAPE) as a concrete alternative: each cached object carries a (priority, deadline, size) tuple, and the eviction scorer is a weighted combination of inverse priority, time-to-deadline slack, and size — empirically reducing KV miss-induced recomputation by ~34% relative to LRU under mixed workloads. The residual hard problem is that deadlines are estimates, and when the arbiter's slot forecast is wrong the eviction policy has protected the wrong tensors — eviction policy correctness is downstream of forecast accuracy, creating a dependency chain where the KV store's efficiency is bounded by the arbiter's prediction quality rather than by its own design.

The shared prefix block cannot be correctly governed by either request's priority in isolation — the block's eviction priority must be the maximum priority among all requests currently referencing it, because evicting it harms the highest-priority dependent regardless of how many low-priority requesters also share it; this is a direct application of the multi-owner resource problem and means priority must be tracked at the block level with a reference set, not at the request level with a pointer to blocks. The concrete implementation requires a reference counting structure augmented with a priority ceiling: each 4KB-16KB KV block (the granularity used in vLLM's prefix caching and Mooncake's block allocator) maintains a sorted set of referencing request priorities, and its effective eviction score uses the maximum element of that set — when the tier-1 request completes and dereferences the block, the ceiling drops to tier-2 and the block becomes eviction-eligible at the lower priority without any explicit policy intervention. What this reveals is that request-level priority is the wrong abstraction for cache management: the correct primitive is block-level priority with dynamic ceiling inheritance, and systems that tag cache entries with the priority of the request that wrote them (the common lazy implementation) will systematically under-protect shared infrastructure blocks that happen to have been written first by a low-priority request but are now on the critical path of a high-priority one. The failure mode of static write-time priority tagging is concrete and severe: in a RAG serving system where a shared system prompt or retrieved context block is first populated by a batch/background tier-3 job, that block gets a tier-3 eviction score permanently, and when a tier-1 interactive request arrives sharing that prefix, the cache may have already evicted the block based on its original low-priority tag — forcing tier-1 recomputation that the cache was explicitly designed to prevent. SGLang's RadixAttention, which organizes prefix blocks in a radix tree, implicitly approaches this problem by making block sharing structurally explicit, but its eviction policy as of mid-2024 still uses LRU at the node level without priority ceiling inheritance — meaning the multi-owner priority problem exists in production systems today. The deeper revelation is that priority is a property of access demand, not of data provenance: the correct eviction framework treats each block's priority as a function of its current reference set's maximum demand, which must be recomputed dynamically as requests arrive and depart rather than assigned once at write time.

The canonical race is a check-then-evict / dereference interleaving: the eviction thread reads a block's priority ceiling as tier-1 (safe, do not evict), the owning tier-1 request concurrently completes and decrements its reference, dropping the ceiling to tier-3, and the eviction thread proceeds to spare the block based on its stale read — this is benign. The dangerous inversion is the reverse ordering: the eviction thread reads the ceiling as tier-3 (eviction candidate), selects the block, and before it executes the eviction, a new tier-1 request arrives and increments the reference set, raising the ceiling to tier-1 — the eviction thread then evicts a block that is now on the critical path of a tier-1 request, causing exactly the recomputation penalty the priority system was designed to prevent. The correct consistency guarantee is eviction atomicity with respect to reference set mutations: the operation sequence (read ceiling → decide to evict → execute eviction) must be atomic with respect to any reference increment, which in practice requires either a per-block reader-writer lock with eviction holding the write lock or a compare-and-swap on a versioned reference count that aborts the eviction if the reference set changed between decision and execution. Memcached and Redis both sidestep this by running single-threaded eviction loops, but a disaggregated KV cache tier serving hundreds of prefill/decode workers needs concurrent eviction throughput, making single-threaded eviction a bottleneck — Mooncake's architecture uses sharded block tables with per-shard locks precisely to parallelize eviction while bounding the atomicity scope. The subtler consistency requirement is priority ceiling downgrade visibility: when a tier-1 request dereferences a block, the ceiling drop must be visible to the eviction thread before the next eviction scan, or the block remains over-protected and occupies space that should have been reclaimed — a stale high ceiling is a memory leak in the eviction policy, not a correctness violation, but under sustained load it degrades to pathological cache bloat where blocks are never evicted because their ceilings are perpetually stale-high. The fundamental tension is that strong atomicity is expensive at the granularity of individual blocks when the cache contains millions of blocks and eviction must run continuously — production systems will be tempted to use epoch-based reclamation or periodic ceiling recomputation, both of which reintroduce a window where the race condition is live, and the correct engineering answer is to bound that window tightly enough that its probability times its recomputation cost is below the SLO budget.
